prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: B017 is the cleanest theory-to-experiment story on the shortlist. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted in 2011 that the moire continuum model has a magic angle where the bandwidth collapses, and Jarillo-Herrero's group showed in 2018 that devices near that angle host correlated insulators and superconductivity tunable by gating. The prediction was specific, the experiment tested it, and the result opened a field (moire quantum materials) that has since been reproduced in many laboratories and extended to other stacks. The three credited names map onto the structure of the discovery without forcing an arbitrary cut, which cannot be said of B010, B042 or B003, where the credited list exceeds three. Seven of eight members ranked it, and four put it in the top three, so the support is broad even if it is not unanimous at the top. I still place it first, as in my opening ballot.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, and several colleagues read that as a sign the field is early. The 2018 experiments were carried out by a team whose first author, Yuan Cao, is not among the credited names, and the contributions of Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and others to the broader moire program are not captured. If the committee decides that the discovery is the existence of the flat-band correlated platform and not the superconductivity, the case is stronger, but a prize this soon could be criticised as favouring one group in a fast, crowded field.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B017 seventh because the interpretation of the superconducting state is still debated and recognition may be somewhat early, and she places optical lattice clocks (B001) first.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously but do not think an open pairing mechanism undermines the discovery being rewarded. The prize can describe the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated and superconducting states, not a settled theory of pairing, and the Nobel record has several cases (high-temperature superconductivity among them) where the mechanism stayed open. Eight years, with reproduction across many groups and platforms, is a normal horizon. Where I agree with her is that B001 is a strong and well-defined candidate, and I keep it as an alternative. My hesitation there is that I cannot judge the metrology details from my own field, and I want the atomic-physics members to say whether it is a distinct step from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube (B027) first as detector-led opening of a new observational window, and ranks B017 seventh as perhaps early.
responses.response: I agree B027 is a real discovery in the sense of finding something new in nature, which is why I ranked it fourth. My objection is attribution. The credited list gives Halzen alone for a collaboration-scale project, and Pearce himself notes that early proposers and builders are missing. A single-name prize for IceCube would be hard to defend unless the committee can show that others are not equally decisive, and the source identifications are still at moderate significance. I would keep B027 as a candidate for later, when the source picture is firmer, and not make it the headline now.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B003) first and calls B017 premature, but also ranks B010 second and B001 third.
responses.response: On B003 I see a serious problem that her own note raises: four credited names, a real Blais versus Girvin question, and a prize in 2025 for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits that makes the area look recently visited. I do not think the committee should reward the same circuit platform twice in two years without strong reason. On B017, her concern that fractional Chern and moire discoveries may need separate recognition later is fair, but it argues for a citation worded narrowly around the magic-angle flat bands and correlated states, which is what I propose.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B001 and B042 and ranks B017 third, noting that the omission of Cao and others complicates attribution and that eight years may be short.
responses.response: I agree with him that Yuan Cao's absence from the credited names is a real problem, and I do not want to hide it. The statutes cap the prize at three persons and the credited names for this candidate are the established ones, so the committee should say openly that the experimental credit goes to the group through its leader. On B042 I differ: his own note says any three-person selection leaves out decisive contributors among five strong ones, and I ranked it eighth for that reason and for overlap with earlier AMO prizes.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B017 first and values the direct meeting of computed band structure and measured transport, and ranks B010 fourth and B015 third.
responses.response: I share the view that B017 is a first-rate theory-experiment match. Where I qualify his enthusiasm is on B015: tunnel magnetoresistance is mature and technologically important, but the credit split between the 1995 room-temperature results and the 2004 MgO advance, with the Yuasa group and the theorists absent, is as unresolved as anything on the list, and the 2007 prize covers much of the neighbouring ground. I would not elevate it above B010, where at least the Kane and Molenkamp core is clear.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the experimental credit for the 2018 discovery rests with the group leader and not the first author.
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism will be judged a bar to maturity at this time.
Whether optical lattice clocks (B001) are seen as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which I cannot judge from my own field.
If B010 is preferred, how to allocate three places among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, given the uncredited Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented ties (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any credited person on the shortlist.
